questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3x+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=3\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)-(x+y)^{3}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)-(1+0)^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 0-{1}^{3} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =-1(y) \\ z+1 & =-y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=2x{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =2(\frac{1}{2}){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi /2)}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ={e}^{0}+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =2(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\pi  \\ z=2x\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,2,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}y+2x-y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-2,2).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =(-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2) \\  & =8-4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,2) & ={f}_{y}(-2,2)(y-2) \\ z-3 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-1$ (or $2y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j+2\,k.$
